title: Alexander Nevsky
description: Grand Prince of Vladimir from 1252 to 1263
wiki_lead:
Alexander Yaroslavich Nevsky (Russian: Александр Ярославич Невский; IPA: [ɐlʲɪˈksandr jɪrɐˈsɫavʲɪtɕ ˈnʲɛfskʲɪj] ; monastic name: Aleksiy; 13 May 1221 – 14 November 1263) was Prince of Novgorod (1236–1240; 1241–1256; 1258–1259) and Grand Prince of Vladimir (1252–1263).
A grandson of Vsevolod the Big Nest, Nevsky rose to legendary status after victories over Swedish invaders in the Battle of the Neva (1240), which earned him the title "Nevsky" in the 15th century, and over German crusaders in the Battle on the Ice (1242). He agreed to pay tribute to the Golden Horde, which allowed him to preserve the Eastern Orthodox Church, while fighting against foreign powers to the west and the south. Macarius, Metropolitan of Moscow canonized Alexander Nevsky as a saint of the Russian Orthodox Church in 1547.
He is considered "one of the great heroes of Russian history", being credited with having "saved the Russian people from Catholicism and being enslaved by the Germans". Although he was already an important figure during his lifetime, his image as the defender of Russia has survived in the centuries after his death. Nevsky's military successes led his image to be used by Peter the Great in the construction of Saint Petersburg. His image was also used to promote patriotism in the Soviet Union, especially during World War II. The 1938 film Alexander Nevsky cemented Nevsky's reputation as a Russian savior. Critics of his legacy argue that the size and importance of his military victories were exaggerated for political purposes, and that he helped ensure the Golden Horde's dominance over Russia.

Alexander Yaroslavich Nevsky (Russian: Александр Ярославич Невский; IPA: [ɐlʲɪˈksandr jɪrɐˈsɫavʲɪtɕ ˈnʲɛfskʲɪj] ; monastic name: Aleksiy; 13 May 1221 – 14 November 1263) was Prince of Novgorod (1236–1240; 1241–1256; 1258–1259) and Grand Prince of Vladimir (1252–1263).

Early life
Alexander was born in Pereslavl-Zalessky on 13 May 1221, although older historiographic tradition placed his date of birth on 30 May 1220. He was the second son of Yaroslav Vsevolodovich, a son of Vsevolod Yuryevich, who was the grand prince of Vladimir. Yaroslav held Pereslavl-Zalessky and the throne of Novgorod during the time of the Mongol conquest in 1237–1238; he inherited the Grand Principality of Vladimir in 1238 following the death of his elder brother, Yury.
There is no consensus regarding the identity of Alexander's mother; her name is given as Feodosiya in Alexander's vita (life). Russian scholarship traditionally identified her as a daughter of Mstislav Mstislavich from Yaroslav's second marriage. Many historians later identified her as a daughter of Ingvar Igorevich of Ryazan from Yaroslav's third marriage after N. A. Baumgarten published an article in 1908 on Alexander's genealogy. However, this hypothesis remains unconfirmed.
He spent most of his youth in Pereslavl-Zalessky. Little is known about the activities of Yaroslav's children before 1238. Alexander is first mentioned indirectly in 1223, when the chronicle of Novgorod records that Yaroslav went to Pereslavl-Zalessky with his children. Alexander is mentioned directly for the first time in 1228, when Yaroslav, who was the prince of Novgorod at the time, left the city for his own domain and left behind his eldest two sons to rule on his behalf. Alexander's eldest brother, Fyodor, died unexpectedly in the summer of 1233 at the age of 14, leaving Alexander as the eldest surviving son.
One of the first known references to Alexander Yaroslavich is in Tales of the Life and Courage of the Pious and Great Prince Alexander in the Pskov Chronicles (c. 1260–1280):

By the will of God, prince Alexander was born from the charitable, people-loving, and meek the Great Prince Yaroslav, and his mother was Theodosia. As it was told by the prophet Isaiah: "Thus sayeth the Lord: I appoint the princes because they are sacred and I direct them."
...He was taller than others and his voice reached the people as a trumpet, and his face was like the face of Joseph, whom the Egyptian Pharaoh placed as next to the king after him of Egypt. His power was a part of the power of Samson and God gave him the wisdom of Solomon... this Prince Alexander: he used to defeat but was never defeated...

grok_lead: Alexander Yaroslavich Nevsky (c. 1221 â 14 November 1263) was a medieval Rus' prince who served as ruler of Novgorod from 1236 to 1252 and grand prince of Vladimir from 1252 until his death, distinguished by defensive campaigns against Scandinavian and Teutonic incursions amid the Mongol conquest of Eastern Europe. His sobriquet "Nevsky" derived from the 1240 victory over Swedish forces led by Birger Jarl at the Battle of the Neva River, where Novgorodian troops under his command disrupted an amphibious landing aimed at establishing a foothold in the Baltic region. Two years later, in 1242, Nevsky's army confronted and defeated an advance by the Livonian Order near Lake Peipus, an engagement chronicled in the Novgorod First Chronicle but later embellished in hagiographic accounts to emphasize a decisive rout on the ice, though contemporary records indicate a tactical repulsion of raiders rather than the mass drowning of knights depicted in legends. Confronting the Golden Horde's suzerainty following their 1237â1240 campaigns that subjugated much of Rus', Nevsky pursued a policy of nominal submission, collecting tribute for the khans and suppressing local revolts to avoid the scorched-earth reprisals that devastated non-compliant principalities, thereby enabling cultural and Orthodox continuity under Mongol oversight. This pragmatic stance, prioritizing survival over ideological resistance, contrasted with futile uprisings elsewhere and facilitated the eventual consolidation of northeastern Rus' principalities. Venerated posthumously for defending Orthodoxy against Latin proselytism, he was formally canonized by the Russian Orthodox Church in 1547, with his relics enshrined as symbols of martial piety.
